brief: Despite anxiety that AI is hurting young workers' job prospects, the youth labor market is strengthening: youth unemployment fell to 9.3% in October 2026, among the lowest in decades, and the youth-overall unemployment gap normalized to a benign 5.2 points. The bank argues the unusually large Gen Z cohort (births peaked at 4.3 million in 2007, rivaling Millennials) explains part of the perceived weakness, since the labor market is taking time to absorb it: youth labor force participation fell from 56.9% (Feb 2023) to 54.4% (Aug 2025) as college enrollment rose from 44.7% to 48.8%, shrinking the labor force by 627,000 even as the youth population grew. But participation has since rebounded sharply to 55.5%, with 653,000 young people joining the labor force from August to October 2026. Separately, the bank raised its 2026/2027 headline inflation forecast to 3.9%/2.3% (Iran-conflict uncertainty lifting the 2027 figure) and still expects a 25bp December hike plus another in Q1 2027, backed by October's inflation print and a stronger-than-expected payrolls report. Risks: oil swings from the Iran conflict, political scrutiny of hyperscaler AI capex, and a potential AI-equity-valuation collapse hitting consumption.
